lead: Prestressing works only if both materials can take very high stress. The concrete must carry a large permanent compression without crushing or splitting, and the steel must hold a high tensile stress for decades while the concrete slowly shortens. That is why prestressed concrete pairs high-strength concrete, usually M40 and above, with high-tensile steel wires, strands and bars of about 1500 to 1900 N/mm² strength. The pair makes long spans, thin sections and crack-free service possible.
prereq: You need the properties of concrete and reinforcing steel (stress-strain curves, Ec = 5000√fck) and the idea of stored compression.

sections.h3: Why ordinary steel fails as a tendon

blocks.text: A tendon of area A<sub>p</sub> stressed to f<sub>p</sub> applies a force P = A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>p</sub>. After transfer the concrete keeps shortening: at once by elastic shortening, then for years by creep and shrinkage. The bonded tendon shortens with it, and every bit of shortening strain ε removes E<sub>s</sub>ε of tendon stress. In a typical beam these three effects together remove 150 to 250 N/mm².
Δf<sub>p</sub> = m f<sub>c</sub> + φ m f<sub>c</sub> + ε<sub>sh</sub> E<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: Δf<sub>p</sub> is the tendon stress lost in N/mm²; m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub> is the modular ratio; f<sub>c</sub> is the concrete stress at tendon level in N/mm²; φ is the creep coefficient; ε<sub>sh</sub> is the shrinkage strain; E<sub>s</sub> is the steel modulus, about 195,000 to 200,000 N/mm².

blocks.text: Mild steel Fe 250 can be stretched to perhaps 200 N/mm². A loss of 150 to 250 N/mm² wipes out almost all of it, which is why the early attempts with ordinary steel failed. High-tensile steel jacked to about 1400 N/mm² loses the same 150 to 250 N/mm² and keeps most of its force. The loss is fixed by the concrete, so the only way to keep the force is to start from a very high steel stress.

Grade M40 means a characteristic cube strength f<sub>ck</sub> of 40 N/mm² at 28 days. IS 1343 asks for at least M40 in pre-tensioned work and permits M30 in post-tensioned work; M40 to M60 is common in bridges and precast plants. The strength at the age of transfer, f<sub>ci</sub>, matters too, because the full prestress often arrives when the concrete is only a few days old.

Stronger concrete helps in five ways. It carries higher compression, so the section can be smaller. Its modulus E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub> is higher (31,600 N/mm² for M40 against 22,400 for M20), so elastic shortening is smaller. It creeps and shrinks less, so the time-dependent losses are smaller. It takes the high bearing stress under anchorage plates. And it gives better bond, so pre-tensioned strands transfer their force over a shorter length. Its flexural tensile strength 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub> also rises with grade (4.4 N/mm² for M40), though it stays a small fraction of the cube strength.

Prestressing steel comes in three forms. A wire is a single cold-drawn wire, 3 to 8 mm, plain or indented (IS 1785 covers plain hard-drawn wire). A strand is a group of wires twisted together; the common 7-wire strand has six wires wound round a straight centre wire. Low-relaxation 7-ply strand (IS 14268) of 12.7 mm nominal size has an area of about 98.7 mm² and a breaking load of about 184 kN, so fpu ≈ 1860 N/mm². A bar is a solid alloy-steel bar, 20 to 40 mm, often threaded for nut anchorages (IS 2090); bars are weaker, around 1000 N/mm².

The stress-strain curve has no yield plateau. It is nearly straight up to about 70 to 80 percent of the strength, then bends gradually and breaks at a small total strain of a few percent. Because there is no yield point, the code uses a proof stress: the stress that leaves a small specified permanent strain after unloading, read with an offset line parallel to the straight part. The jacking stress is capped at about three-quarters of fpu so the tendon stays in the near-elastic range.

Relaxation is the slow loss of stress in steel held at constant length; it grows with the initial stress and the temperature. It is not creep: creep is strain growing under constant stress, relaxation is stress falling under constant strain. Low-relaxation strand, made by stretching the strand while it is heated, loses roughly half as much as ordinary stress-relieved strand. The numbers belong to losses of prestress.

examples.question: A pre-tensioned beam of M40 concrete has a concrete stress at tendon level of f<sub>c</sub> = 8 N/mm² after transfer. Take E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm², creep coefficient φ = 1.6 and shrinkage strain 300 × 10⁻⁶. (a) Find the stress lost by elastic shortening, creep and shrinkage. (b) Compare what is left in a mild-steel tendon stretched to 200 N/mm² and in a 1860 N/mm² strand jacked to 0.75 f<sub>pu</sub>. (c) With a further relaxation loss of 35 N/mm², how many 12.7 mm strands (98.7 mm² each) give an effective force of 900 kN?
steps: Modulus of concrete: E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√40 = 31,623 N/mm². Modular ratio m = 195,000/31,623 = 6.17.
(b) Mild steel: 200 − 186.8 = 13.2 N/mm² left, only 7 percent of the initial stress. Strand: jacking stress 0.75 × 1860 = 1,395 N/mm²; 1,395 − 186.8 = 1,208.2 N/mm² left, 87 percent.
(c) Effective strand stress = 1,395 − 186.8 − 35 = 1,173.2 N/mm². Area needed = 900,000/1,173.2 = 767 mm². Strands = 767/98.7 = 7.77, so provide 8 strands (789.6 mm², effective force 926 kN).
examples.answer: Losses 49.3 + 78.9 + 58.5 = 186.8 N/mm². A mild-steel tendon would keep only 13.2 N/mm² (7 percent), useless as prestress; the strand keeps 1,208.2 N/mm² (87 percent). 8 strands of 12.7 mm give the 900 kN effective force.

traps: Using 250 N/mm² or the yield stress of mild steel as if it applied to prestressing steel. High-tensile steel has no yield point; the code works with f<sub>pu</sub> and a proof stress.
Reading M40 as a tensile strength. It is the characteristic cube compressive strength at 28 days; the flexural tensile strength of M40 is only about 4.4 N/mm².
Writing that strong concrete "resists" shrinkage. Higher grades simply creep and shrink less, so the losses are smaller.
Confusing relaxation with creep: relaxation is stress loss in the steel at constant strain; creep is strain growth in the concrete at constant stress.
Mixing units: mm² × N/mm² gives N. Divide by 1000 only at the end to get kN.

quiz.a: A characteristic cube compressive strength of 40 N/mm² at 28 days, on 150 mm cubes: the strength that not more than 5 percent of results are expected to fall below.

quiz.q: Name the three forms of prestressing steel and give a typical strength of each.
quiz.a: Wire (about 1500 to 1700 N/mm²), 7-wire strand (about 1860 N/mm²) and high-tensile alloy bar (about 1000 N/mm²).

quiz.q: Why did early attempts at prestressing with mild steel fail?
quiz.a: Elastic shortening, creep and shrinkage of concrete remove 150 to 250 N/mm² of steel stress. Mild steel could only be stretched to about 200 N/mm², so almost all of the prestress was lost within months.

quiz.q: Why is a proof stress used for prestressing steel?
quiz.a: Its stress-strain curve has no yield plateau, so a proof stress, the stress that leaves a small specified permanent strain on unloading, takes the place of a yield stress.

quiz.q: A tendon of 7 strands of 12.7 mm (98.7 mm² each) is jacked to 1395 N/mm². Find the jacking force.
Find E<sub>c</sub> and the modular ratio for M50 concrete with E<sub>s</sub> = 195 kN/mm².

In the worked example, the grade is raised from M40 to M60 with the same f<sub>c</sub>, φ and ε<sub>sh</sub>. By how much does the elastic shortening plus creep loss fall, and what else would change in practice?
quiz.a: E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√60 = 38,730 N/mm², m = 5.03. (1 + φ) m f<sub>c</sub> = 2.6 × 5.03 × 8 = 104.7 N/mm² against 128.3 N/mm², a fall of 23.5 N/mm². In practice φ and ε<sub>sh</sub> are also lower for the richer, denser mix, so the real saving is larger, and the section could be made smaller.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most new strand is low-relaxation 7-wire strand of 12.7 or 15.2 mm, often greased and sheathed for unbonded slabs. Ultra-high-performance concrete, above 150 N/mm², is used in thin precast footbridges and joints. Corrosion of strands in poorly grouted ducts has led to tendon replacements on several bridges worldwide, so grout quality is now tested and recorded. Search for low-relaxation strand, ultra-high-performance concrete and grouting of post-tensioned ducts.
